idea: The Beaufort scale as a column of 13 tiny drawn sea surfaces, from a glassy line at Force 0 to a churned white sea at Force 12, with just 'Force 0' at the top and 'Force 12: Hurricane' at the bottom. For anyone who has stood on a pier and wondered how bad it really was.

Luke Howard's 1802 cloud classification as a vertical altitude chart with ruled sky, drawn in code: cirrus, cumulus, stratus, nimbus in their layers, captioned 'Named in 1802 by a pharmacist.' Looking up becomes reading.
Five stages of a river meander cutting itself off into an oxbow lake, plan-view lines in sequence, captioned 'A river changing its mind.' A calm, true diagram for people who like slow patient change.

The lobes of the Mississippi delta drawn as overlapping fans, each a former course of the river, with the caption 'It has never stayed put.' The river has shifted its mouth every thousand years or so; the point of view is that maps of rivers are always temporary.

Raindrops sorted by size in a row, from drizzle to the largest drops of about 5 mm, each drawn to scale with its fall speed beside it (roughly 2 m/s up to 9 m/s), captioned 'Rain, sorted.' Quiet, exact, and slightly absurd.

A Nakaya-style chart of snow crystal shapes by temperature, a grid of plates, needles, columns and dendrites drawn in code, captioned 'Same sky. Different weather. Different snowflake.' Shows that every flake records the air it fell through.

A lightning stepped leader drawn as a branching line descending in short segments toward the ground, captioned 'The path is chosen before the flash.' The visible bolt is the return stroke; the decision was made in the dark steps first.

The water cycle drawn as a plain flow chart with average waiting times in each box: atmosphere about 9 days, oceans about 3,000 years. Caption: 'Everything you drink is waiting its turn.' A cycle with a sense of patience.

Buys Ballot's law as a drawn cyclone with isobars and a tiny figure standing back to the wind, captioned 'Back to the wind, low pressure on your left.' True in the Northern Hemisphere, and a rule a sailor can use.

The Hjulström curve redrawn as a clean log-log chart of flow speed against grain size, showing where a river erodes, carries or drops its load, captioned 'Clay is the hardest thing to pick up.' A counter-intuitive fact for people who like being surprised by physics.

A flood hydrograph, two curves on one graph: a sharp rainfall bar chart above and the river's slower rise and fall below, with the gap marked 'lag time' and captioned 'The river hears about the rain later.' A joke about delayed consequences.

A cooling-air diagram showing temperature falling toward the dew point through a night, ending in a ground-level cloud, captioned 'Fog is a cloud that touches the ground.' Short, true and a bit wry for anyone who has driven through it.

Franklin and Folger's 1770 Gulf Stream chart redrawn as a one-ink line map, the current as a ribbon crossing the Atlantic, captioned 'Why the mail ship was slower.' It is the first published chart of the stream and shows a founding father doing oceanography.

A mercury barometer in cross-section, a tube standing in a dish with the column marked at 760 mm, captioned 'The whole sky, weighed.' The atmosphere's weight above you holds up that column at standard sea-level pressure.

Spring and neap tide geometry drawn from above: Sun, Moon and Earth in line on one side, at right angles on the other, with 'Bay of Fundy: up to 16 m, twice a day' beneath. For anyone who likes knowing what the sea is doing and why.

A ship's Plimsoll load line mark with its lettered lines (TF, F, T, S, W, WNA) drawn to scale on a hull section, captioned 'How low a ship may sit, by law.' A reminder that overloaded ships sank until Plimsoll's 1876 act.

A Strahler stream-order diagram: first-order trickles joining into a branching river drawn as a tree of lines in code, captioned 'Every river is made of smaller rivers.' Beautiful as a pattern, with a gentle point about scale.

A mountain cross-section showing wet wind rising on one side, raining out, and descending dry on the other, captioned 'Rain shadow: one side of the hill gets all of it.' Works for anyone who ever felt they were on the wrong slope.
A hailstone cut in half, drawn with its concentric growth rings, captioned 'One ring per trip up the storm.' Hail is built as it is carried up and down a thundercloud, so the stone is its own diary.

A bar chart of river discharge with the Amazon's bar so tall it runs off the shirt, the next rivers shrinking beside it, captioned 'Roughly a fifth of all the river water that reaches the sea.' A one-glance statement of scale.
